newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM to forgo Aug 15 visit to war shrine.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM to forgo Aug 15 visit to war shrine.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who is scheduled to visit China next month, will not visit a controversial Tokyo war shrine to mark the anniversary of the end of World War Two, a government spokesman said on Tuesday.
"The prime minister will not visit Yasukuni Shrine on August 15," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference.

Hashimoto, who is scheduled to visit China from September 4-7, had earlier rebuffed a call by the right-wing of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) to visit the central Tokyo shrine on the 52nd anniversary of the war's end.
"My feelings about Yasukuni Shrine are perhaps even stronger than yours, but present circumstances make it difficult," Hashimoto, LDP president, told his colleagues.

Hashimoto's China trip will take place just before Japan begins a comprehensive review of its military alliance with the United States with the aim of increasing Tokyo's security role in its region. China is extremely sensitive about the scheme.
Yasukuni Shrine is the main shrine of Shinto, Japan's indigenous animistic faith, dedicated to the country's 2.6 million war dead since the 19th century.

The shrine is as reviled by Asians who suffered Japanese invasion as it is revered by Japan's nationalists because it houses the spirits of Class-A war criminals including the wartime prime minister, General Hideki Tojo.

Annual visits to Yasukuni by cabinet ministers trigger bitter criticism from China and other Asian countries, as Hashimoto himself discovered after he paid respects at the shrine on July 29, 1996, to mark his 59th birthday.

Seven ministers of Hashimoto's 20-member cabinet intend to visit Yasukuni on August 15, while several others had already gone there or would go on different days, Kyodo news agency reported on Tuesday.
On Monday, foreign ministry officials said Hashimoto's China trip would include a visit to a war museum in the northeastern Chinese city of Shenyang which documents Japanese atrocities.

He would be the first Japanese prime minister to visit northeastern China, which suffered chemical weapons attacks, cruel biological experiments on live prisoners and scorched-earth tactics during Japan's invasion beginning in the early 1930s.
